endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Address how responsibility shifts if the tool is modified in ways that change its regulatory classification.

commentary.bottom_line: No study tests whether contract clauses requiring vendor notice of FDA classification changes, or defining how responsibility shifts, reduce unrecognized liability transfer to health systems. The recommendation rests on a single governance framework, the CHAI playbooks, which lists it as a must.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The only support is expert consensus expressed in one framework, which reflects judgment rather than observed outcomes.

The CHAI governance playbooks direct organizations to address how responsibility shifts if a tool is modified in ways that change its regulatory classification. No study in this map examines how often such reclassifications occur, whether vendors disclose them, or whether contract terms change who bears liability when they do.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that document how often AI tools undergo modifications that change FDA classification after purchase, whether health systems learn of these changes, and whether contracts with notification and responsibility clauses lead to earlier awareness, renegotiation, or different liability outcomes than contracts without them.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have less legal and contracting capacity to negotiate such clauses, but this remains untested.
